title: YouTube Outro Script: 36 Ready-to-Use Endings That Lead to the Next Video
markdown:
# YouTube Outro Script: 36 Ready-to-Use Endings That Lead to the Next Video

The camera is off, the edit is nearly exported, and the last 20 seconds are still empty. That small gap can hold up an upload longer than the shoot did. This guide gives you ready-to-adapt YouTube outro scripts, plus a simple way to choose an ending that matches the video you just made and the next one you want viewers to watch.

A good outro has one job at a time: close the promise of the current video, then give the viewer a specific reason to continue. Use one of the lines below as a draft, replace the bracketed details, and say it in your own voice.

## Tutorial and education outros

1. “You now have the first step: [SKILL OR RESULT]. Next, watch [NEXT VIDEO] to avoid the mistake that slows most beginners down.”

2. “Before you leave, try this once: [ONE ACTION]. Then continue with [NEXT VIDEO] when you’re ready for the full process.”

3. “That is the framework. In the next video, I’ll show you what it looks like when [COMMON COMPLICATION] happens.”

4. “If [TOPIC] felt complicated before this video, save this checklist: [THREE-WORD SUMMARY]. The next lesson is [NEXT VIDEO].”

5. “Your homework is simple: do [ACTION] before [TIME OR TRIGGER]. Then watch [NEXT VIDEO] for the part most tutorials skip.”

6. “We covered the ‘what.’ The video on screen covers the ‘how’ with a complete [PROJECT OR EXAMPLE].”

7. “Pick one idea from this video and test it today. When you do, come back for [NEXT VIDEO], where we build on it.”

8. “The key is not [COMMON MISCONCEPTION]; it is [CORRECT PRINCIPLE]. For the next move, watch [NEXT VIDEO].”

9. “If you are starting from zero, begin with this video again. If you are ready to improve [SPECIFIC SKILL], the next video is for you.”

10. “That is the fast version. The video on screen gives you the slower walkthrough, including [MISSING DETAIL].”

## Product review and comparison outros

11. “My pick for [USE CASE] is [OPTION], but your answer changes if [CONDITION]. Watch the comparison on screen before you decide.”

12. “Do not buy based on one feature. Compare [FACTOR ONE], [FACTOR TWO], and [FACTOR THREE] in the next video.”

13. “If you already own [PRODUCT], start with [ACTION]. If you are choosing between options, the next video breaks down the trade-offs.”

14. “This is the right choice for [AUDIENCE]. For [DIFFERENT AUDIENCE], click the video on screen instead.”

15. “The short answer is [PRODUCT OR VERDICT]. The longer answer—including the limitation I would plan around—is in [NEXT VIDEO].”

16. “Before checkout, ask yourself one question: [QUESTION]. Then use the next video to compare the answers.”

17. “I would not choose [OPTION] for [CONDITION]. Watch [NEXT VIDEO] if that is your situation.”

18. “The feature list is not the whole story. The next video shows what [PRODUCT OR CATEGORY] is like after [REAL USE PERIOD OR TASK].”

## Creator and behind-the-scenes outros

19. “That is how this video came together, from [STARTING POINT] to [RESULT]. Next, I’ll show the part that almost did not make the cut: [NEXT TOPIC].”

20. “If you want the setup behind this result, the next video walks through [TOOLS, PROCESS, OR DECISION].”

21. “The finished version looks simple because [HIDDEN WORK]. Click through for the workflow I use before I press record.”

22. “This was version [ADD: version number], not the first attempt. The next video shows what I changed and why.”

23. “You have seen the final shot. Now watch [NEXT VIDEO] for the planning that made it possible.”

24. “The lesson from this project is [LESSON]. I put the next experiment on screen if you want to see whether it holds up.”

25. “I will use [PROCESS] again, with one change: [CHANGE]. The next video explains that decision.”

26. “If your own project is stuck at [STAGE], start with the next video. It is built for that exact moment.”

## Story, commentary, and essay outros

27. “That is why [CENTRAL IDEA] matters now. The next video follows the question it leaves behind: [NEXT QUESTION].”

28. “The important part is not that [EVENT OR IDEA] happened. It is what changed afterward. Continue with [NEXT VIDEO] for that chapter.”

29. “There is one detail I left out because it needs its own story: [DETAIL]. That story is next.”

30. “If this changed how you see [TOPIC], the next video takes the argument one step further.”

31. “We started with [OPENING IMAGE OR QUESTION]. We end with [ANSWER OR TENSION]. For the next piece of the puzzle, watch [NEXT VIDEO].”

32. “This is not the final word on [TOPIC]. It is the starting point for [NEXT VIDEO].”

33. “The pattern is clear: [SHORT PATTERN]. The next video asks where that pattern breaks.”

34. “Keep this question in mind: [QUESTION]. It is the starting line of the video on screen.”

## Challenge, fitness, and transformation outros

35. “Today’s target was [TARGET]. Your next step is [NEXT ACTION], and the next video shows how to do it without [COMMON SETBACK].”

36. “Do not judge the result by one day. Track [MEASURE] for [ADD: time period], then watch [NEXT VIDEO] for the next phase.”

## How to choose the right ending

Start with the state of the viewer at the final frame.

- If they have just learned something, point to the next skill or the common complication.
- If they are deciding what to buy, point to the comparison or the condition that changes the recommendation.
- If they have followed a story, point to the unresolved question rather than repeating the conclusion.
- If they have completed a challenge or plan, name the next action and the next phase.

Keep the spoken ending narrow. “Watch another video” gives no reason to move. “Watch the comparison if you edit on a phone” gives a viewer with that problem a clear destination.

Match the end-screen choice to the line. If you say “the comparison,” show the comparison. If you say “the next lesson,” show the lesson. Remove any sentence that asks for an action you do not make easy to take.

## How to test a YouTube outro script

Write two endings for the same video, each leading to a different but genuinely relevant next video. Keep the current video’s conclusion the same; change only the bridge.

For example:

- Version A: “Now that you can [CURRENT RESULT], watch [NEXT VIDEO] to handle [NEXT PROBLEM].”
- Version B: “Before you try [CURRENT RESULT], watch [NEXT VIDEO] to avoid [COMMON MISTAKE].”

Use one version for a future upload, note the exact wording and destination, then compare it with another relevant ending on a comparable future upload. Look for a useful editorial signal: did the ending clearly finish the current promise, and did the suggested video make sense to the person who reached it? Do not turn a single result into a rule. The better line is the one that stays honest to the video and creates a clearer next choice.

## FAQ

### How long should a YouTube outro script be?

Long enough to close the current idea and introduce one next action. If your ending contains several asks, cut it down to the most relevant one.

### Should every video point to another video?

When you have a genuinely related next video, it is a useful destination. If you do not, end cleanly rather than forcing an unrelated recommendation.

### What should I say before the end screen?

Name the specific viewer, benefit, or question in the next video. Then make sure the displayed video matches what you said.

### Can I use the same outro on every upload?

A recurring sign-off can build familiarity, but the bridge into the next video should change with the topic. Specificity is what makes an outro useful.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the kind of brief and deliverables you can use:

**You send:** "Write an 8-minute video for self-taught beginners about five mistakes when learning to code. Tone: encouraging but direct."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Titles (3) + one thumbnail-text idea.**
- **Hooks (3, first 15 seconds):** e.g. "You're not bad at coding. You're making these five mistakes." plus the explicit promise the opening makes.
- **Timestamped script** with `[B-ROLL: ...]` and `[ON-SCREEN: ...]` cues, built around open/close loops and pacing changes.
- **CTA + end-screen transition** into a next-video tease.
- **Notes:** pacing, the first A/B test to run, and any missing facts marked `[ADD: ...]`.
